turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): In you come, up on the couch there. I'll have this dressing off before he's even out of that login screen. Ten days since the section, am I right?

[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Ten days yesterday, the emergency caesarean, twenty-two hours of labour and then straight to theatre. Little Oisín is a dote, feeding every two hours, but the scar, I've been worrying at it since the weekend, turning it over and over.
[SEG0003] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sorry, one second, it's kicked me out again. The operation, say the timing again, I missed it.

[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Ten days ago, emergency caesarean for failure to progress. I'm after coming in because the wound has gone fierce red, and I want someone to look before I talk myself into a panic.
[SEG0005] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Nuala, the live-in carer, I'm with her till the end of the month while the husband is on the sites in Cork. The redness is worse than she'll admit if you let her talk.
[SEG0006] person_3 (DOCTOR): Nuala, grand. The redness, how long? Say it again, I was clicking the wrong chart.
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Two days. Wednesday morning, out of the shower, the skin at the left end of the scar was pink, just a patch, not the whole length of it, I measured it with my fingers.
[SEG0008] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Saturday. I saw it red on Saturday when I did the top dressing, and that's four days. She was up to her eyes with the bottles.
[SEG0009] person_3 (DOCTOR): Two days, four days, sure it's a few days. Any pain in the wound?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No pain at all. The spinal wore off before I left the hospital and since I got home it's been grand, not a bother, I haven't given it a thought.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any discharge, any muck on the dressing? Hang on, say it once the letter loads. Actually you haven't said it yet.

[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No, I don't think so. I checked the outside of the dressing at seven this morning and it was dry, maybe a pink mark from the tape, but nothing wet, I was very careful looking.

[SEG0013] person_1 (NURSE): Dressing's off. Yellow-green discharge at the left angle, redness and warmth about three centimetres round it, the edges are still together with no gaping, and there's a small bit of a smell off it.

[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah here, now I can see it. There was a wet yellow patch on the pyjama top last night and I told myself it was sweat, but that's the same colour, so yes there is discharge, it's been seeping since yesterday evening.
[SEG0015] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I saw the patch in the wash. I nearly rang the surgery last night and then the baby settled and I left it.
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sorry, I was squinting at an old haemoglobin on the screen. The colour of the discharge, once more?
[SEG0017] person_1 (NURSE): Yellow-green, left angle. I'll leave the swab pack to one side.

[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Since you've that haemoglobin up, on day two the midwife told me it was borderline, ninety-eight or something around that, not low enough for a transfusion, and they didn't start iron, they said it'd come up on its own. I wrote it on the back of the discharge leaflet so I wouldn't lose it.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): I won't take a remembered ninety-eight as a result, it isn't on this screen. Any vomiting?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No vomiting. I was queasy in the hospital from the morphine, but that was days ago and it's gone, nothing since I came home, not even with the nappies.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): Waterworks, bowels, breathing, any of that at you?

[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Waterworks are fine, no burning and I'm not going more often. The bowels are slow, I was going to blame iron but they never gave me iron, it was the codeine, and I haven't had codeine since day three. Breathing is grand, I can do the landing without stopping.
[SEG0023] person_4 (CAREGIVER): And before I forget, my own ramipril is in the bathroom press, five milligrams, for my blood pressure. Don't be putting them into her box, they're mine, not hers.

[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): And my sister Áine left her biotin on the dresser, the strong hair ones, I nearly swallowed one because the bottles are the same shape, but I read the label and I didn't take it. My father has type 2 diabetes and he takes metformin, a thousand milligrams I think, but that's his sugar, I've never had diabetes myself.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): We'll leave the biotin and your father's metformin and Nuala's ramipril out of the chart. Did you have a temperature with this?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No temperature. I've been checking on account of the baby and it's been normal every time, I wouldn't miss a fever, I'm very particular about the thermometer.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): What antibiotic did they send you home on? The discharge letter is about two millimetres high on this yoke.
[SEG0028] person_1 (NURSE): I've the summary. Co-amoxiclav 625 milligrams by mouth three times a day for seven days, and she was to finish the course.

[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Five days... or was it seven? I finished the box, the last tablet was Thursday, or maybe Wednesday after the two o'clock feed, I cannot pin the day at all. And I'm nearly certain those tablets were 500 milligrams, not 625. The chemist was talking while Oisín was crying, so I might have it wrong, I just don't know.

[SEG0030] person_4 (CAREGIVER): The box in the press said seven days. She missed at least two doses though, one the evening the public health nurse called and one when she fell asleep on the couch, so she didn't take them the way they were written.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): Five or seven days, 500 or 625, and doses missed. I'm not going to tidy that into something it isn't. The dose, say it again, the screen jumped.
[SEG0032] person_1 (NURSE): Summary says 625 three times a day. She's saying 500. The box isn't with us.

[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): I did take them by mouth with food, they warned me the clavulanic acid can turn the stomach, and I was worried about thrush because Oisín is exclusively breastfed, every two to three hours, day and night, which is half the reason the days have blurred into one.
[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): Breastfeeding, I got that much. Any allergy to penicillin, or to anything else?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): No allergies. Not penicillin, not anything. They asked me six times on the labour ward and it's still no, nothing, not even a rash as a child.
[SEG0036] person_1 (NURSE): Vitals while ye sort that. Temperature 37.9 degrees, pulse 98, oxygen 98 percent, respiratory rate 16, blood pressure 132 over 84.

[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): That blood pressure is wrong. I did the home cuff this morning, twice, sitting, and it was 118 over 70 both times. Your machines always read me high, they did it all through the antenatal clinic, I could give you the full history of the cuffs.
[SEG0038] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I was there, the home one said 118 over 70. Those wrist cuffs are desperate, mind, I wouldn't stake the house on either reading.
[SEG0039] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sorry, the pressure, again? I was typing the allergy. 132 over 84 here, 118 over 70 at home. We'll write both down, I'm not repeating it while this is frozen.

[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): And about last night, I know I said there was no temperature, and that wasn't the full truth. Around two in the morning I woke roasting, thermometer under the tongue was 38.4, I was sweating and my teeth were nearly chattering, and it eased after two paracetamol. I didn't want to wake the whole house, the baby had only just gone over.

[SEG0041] person_4 (CAREGIVER): She showed me the 38.4 in the morning. The two paracetamol were the 500 milligram tablets, so a gram, and that's her usual, a gram by mouth four times a day since she came home, for the afterpains and the scar.

[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, paracetamol, a gram four times a day, I have an alarm for it, not like the antibiotic. And since you asked about pain, I wasn't straight. When I cough or when I lift Oisín there's a sharp pull along the left side of the scar, a five out of ten, there since about day three. I decided it was normal healing and not worth mentioning, which was stupid of me.
[SEG0043] person_3 (DOCTOR): Five out of ten, left side, cough and lifting. Let me actually look at it, if the chair will turn.

[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): Red and warm at the left end, a small amount of yellow discharge, and the rest of the wound is dry and closed. I'm treating it as a wound infection, probably a bit of cellulitis, though it could still be a stitch reaction. I can't be sure till we see what the swab grows.

[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): They did mention a stitch reaction on the ward, if it went pink, and they said if it wept or I got a fever I was to come back, which is why I'm here. I've the maternity notes in the big folder as well, three pages of operation note, the registrar was your man with the beard.

[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): We'll swab the wound now and send it. I'm changing you to flucloxacillin for the wound infection, 500 milligrams by mouth four times a day for seven days. It's fine with the breastfeeding. Finish the lot even if the redness fades.
[SEG0047] person_1 (NURSE): I'll take the swab before the new dressing. Do you want bloods in the room as well?
[SEG0048] person_3 (DOCTOR): No bloods today. If the fever spikes again, or she's no better in two days, then a full blood count and a CRP. Otherwise the swab is enough.

[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): If I'm worse tonight, my husband has the Toyota in Cork so I've no car, do I wait the two days or do I go to A&E? I overthink, I know, my mother says I should have done law.

[SEG0050] person_3 (DOCTOR): If the redness spreads, you start vomiting, or you feel worse overnight, go to A&E, don't sit on it. Otherwise I'll see you back here in two days, and bring Nuala's note of any temperatures. She can book it at reception on the way out.
[SEG0051] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I'll book the two days, and I'll write the temperatures on a proper page this time, not the back of a receipt. We'll get a cup of tea once the swab is done.
[SEG0052] person_1 (NURSE): Swab's taken, fresh dressing on, nice and loose. You're grand to go.

spec.situation: Patient 10 days after a hernia, appendix or caesarean operation; wound redness and discharge, fever the night before; nurse removes dressing and describes it; patient is vague about antibiotic course ('five days... or was it seven'); wound swab and antibiotic change.
features: test_result_recalled: the patient reports an old test or result ('they said it was borderline'); recorded as reported history/investigation only as far as said, not as a confirmed value.

denial_then_admission: the patient first denies a symptom, then later describes it. The label records the symptom as present (the later, fuller answer) and does NOT also record the earlier denial as a negative finding.
disputed_numbers: the nurse reads a value and the patient or relative disagrees or remembers another (a dose, a weight, a BP). Keep both and record an uncertainty.

third_party_medicine: someone mentions a medicine or condition that belongs to a relative or friend (the sister's biotin, the husband's metformin). It must not appear as the patient's own; a relative's illness can only be family history if said as such.
spec.doctor_style: distracted by the computer, asks for repeats
